page.title: Event run of show vs in house team decision guide
page.description: Compare run of show structure with in-house team roles, rehearsal plans, escalation paths and tool choices for virtual and hybrid events.
page.h1: How do you decide between a run of show and an in-house team for events?
page.definition: A run of show is a detailed timeline that sequences every cue, speaker and technical switch for a live event, while an in-house team consists of internal staff who execute that plan or produce the event without external crew.
page.quick_answer: Start with a written run of show for every event; assign each cue to a named owner, then decide whether your internal staff can cover all roles or if you need a dedicated producer, show caller and platform operator.

sections.h2: What is the difference between a run of show and an in-house team?

blocks.p: A run of show is a living document that lists every segment, transition, graphic cue and backup plan in chronological order, while an in-house team is the group of people who operate the platform, manage speakers and handle audience interaction during the live event.

ul: Run of show defines what happens and when; in-house team defines who does it.
Run of show is created before rehearsal; in-house team is assembled before production.
Run of show can be reused across events; in-house team capacity changes with workload.
Run of show includes escalation triggers; in-house team executes those triggers.

sections.h2: When should you build a run of show internally versus hiring a production crew?

blocks.p: Build the run of show internally when the event format is repeatable, the platform is familiar and the internal staff have bandwidth for cue calling, speaker management and backup streaming.

ul: Event is a recurring webinar series with a stable agenda.
Team includes a trained producer who can call cues on the platform.
Budget limits external crew to only high-stakes summits.
Risk tolerance allows a single point of failure for technical switching.

blocks.p: Hire a production crew when the event is a summit, hybrid conference or executive briefing that demands a show caller, dedicated platform operator, speaker manager and redundant stream.

sections.h2: How do you rehearse and escalate with each approach?

blocks.p: Both models require a full rehearsal on the real platform two to five days before the event and a technical check sixty minutes before going live, but the escalation path differs.

ol: Schedule a full walk-through with every speaker using the exact platform link.
Assign a cue caller to read the run of show aloud while the operator executes each transition.
Document any timing drift and adjust the run of show immediately.
Define escalation triggers: audio loss, speaker disconnect, platform error.
Name a single decision maker for each trigger and share contact details in a shared channel.

blocks.p: With an external crew the show caller owns escalation; with an in-house team the senior marketing manager or IT lead owns it.

sections.h2: What tools and timelines support each model?

blocks.p: Choose tools that match the complexity of the run of show and the size of the in-house team, then lock the timeline early.

ul: Project plan in Asana, Monday.com or Airtable for the calendar and task owners.
Run of show drafted in Google Docs or Notion with version history.
Platform selection from Zoom Webinars, Microsoft Teams, ON24 or StreamYard.
Registration via Eventbrite or Cvent; follow-up in HubSpot or Salesforce.
Backup stream configured on a secondary encoder or cloud ingest.

blocks.p: Typical lead time is six to eight weeks for a summit or online conference and three to four weeks for a webinar; a repeat format can move faster.

faq.q: Can a single person serve as both show caller and platform operator?
faq.a: Only for simple webinars with one speaker and no backup stream; summits and hybrid events need separate people to avoid missed cues during technical issues.

faq.q: How do you handle a speaker who refuses to rehearse?
faq.a: Flag the speaker in the run of show as unrehearsed, assign a dedicated speaker manager to run a private tech check, and prepare a pre-recorded fallback segment.

faq.q: What is the minimum run of show for a recurring webinar?
faq.a: A one-page timeline with segment start times, speaker names, graphic cues, Q&A windows and a backup stream link, updated each cycle.

faq.q: When should you bring in an external producer for an in-house team?
faq.a: When the event adds a second stage, hybrid audience, simultaneous translation or a backup stream requirement that exceeds internal bandwidth.
